items.explanation: CURRENT_DATE is a date; NOW() is a timestamptz fixed at transaction start.
items.example: SELECT CURRENT_DATE AS today, NOW() AS now_ts;
items.expected: One row with today's date and timestamp.

items.explanation: Returns numeric; ISODOW gives 1 = Monday to 7 = Sunday.
items.example: SELECT order_id, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS y, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) AS m, EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM order_date) AS dow FROM orders LIMIT 5;
items.expected: 5 orders with year, month and weekday.

items.explanation: Rounds down to the start of the period (PostgreSQL).
items.example: SELECT date_trunc('month', order_date)::date AS month, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 5;
items.expected: Order counts for the first 5 months.

items.explanation: date minus date is an integer number of days in PostgreSQL.
items.example: SELECT order_id, shipped_date - order_date AS days_to_ship FROM orders WHERE shipped_date IS NOT NULL LIMIT 5;

items.explanation: Adds calendar units; the result is a timestamp unless cast.
items.example: SELECT order_date, (order_date + interval '1 month')::date AS one_month_later FROM orders LIMIT 5;
items.expected: Order dates shifted by one month.

items.explanation: Returns an interval like '3 years 2 mons'.
items.example: SELECT first_name, AGE(hire_date, birth_date) AS age_at_hire FROM employees;

items.explanation: Formats dates as text. 'Day' pads with spaces; use 'FMDay' to trim.
items.example: SELECT order_id, TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY-MM') AS ym, TO_CHAR(order_date, 'FMDay') AS weekday FROM orders LIMIT 5;
items.expected: 5 orders with year-month and weekday name.

items.explanation: Half-open ranges are index-friendly and handle timestamps correctly.
items.example: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE order_date >= (SELECT MIN(order_date) FROM orders) AND order_date < (SELECT MIN(order_date) FROM orders) + interval '3 months';
items.expected: Orders in the first three months of data.

items.explanation: Builds a list of dates to fill gaps (PostgreSQL).
items.example: SELECT generate_series(DATE '2024-01-01', DATE '2024-01-07', interval '1 day')::date AS d;
